paragraphs.heading: A measure of spread
paragraphs.text: Variance measures dispersion: how far a set of numbers is spread out from its average. Formally, it is the expected value of the square of each deviation from the mean. Take the square root of the variance and you get the standard deviation.

paragraphs.heading: The formula
paragraphs.text: For a random variable X with mean μ = E [X], the variance is Var (X) = E [(X − μ)²]. This covers variables that come from discrete, continuous, mixed or other processes. It can also be read as the covariance of X with itself, Var (X) = Cov (X, X), and is often written σ², s² or Var (X). Another form: take the average of X², then subtract the square of the average of X. That form should not be used with floating-point arithmetic, though, because it suffers from catastrophic cancellation when the two parts are close in size.

paragraphs.heading: Strengths and weaknesses
paragraphs.text: Compared with other measures of spread, like the expected absolute deviation, variance is easier to handle with algebra. To give one case, when random variables are uncorrelated, the variance of their sum equals the sum of their variances. One drawback is that its units differ from those of the variable, which is why the standard deviation is usually reported once the work is done. Another is that many distributions do not have a finite variance.

paragraphs.heading: Two meanings of variance
paragraphs.text: The word names two different things. One belongs to a theoretical probability distribution and comes from an equation. The other describes a set of observations: if you have every possible observation it is the population variance, but usually you have only a subset, giving the sample variance, which serves as an estimate. The two are closely linked. If a distribution generated an infinite number of observations, their sample variance would match the value from the distribution's equation.

paragraphs.heading: Never negative
paragraphs.text: Variance can never be negative, since squares are positive or zero. If a random variable has variance 0, it is almost surely a constant that always takes the same value. A distribution with no finite expected value, such as the Cauchy distribution, cannot have a finite variance either. Yet a finite expected value does not guarantee a finite variance: a Pareto distribution with index k where 1 < k ≤ 2 is an example.

paragraphs.heading: Splitting variance into parts
paragraphs.text: Variance plays a central role in statistics, from descriptive statistics and inference to hypothesis testing, goodness of fit and Monte Carlo sampling. One useful result is the law of total variance: for two random variables X and Y, provided X has a variance, Var [X] equals E (Var [X∣Y]) plus Var (E [X∣Y]). Analysis of variance uses a similar split, 𝑀𝑆_total = 𝑀𝑆_between + 𝑀𝑆_within, where 𝑀𝑆 stands for the mean of the squares.
